Choose neighbors, is a partly non for profit start up, helping people have more fulfilling lives and activities, and to help make money for investors by adding value to property and peoples wallets, by lives, work, projects, affordable homes and services, and to encourage people to migrate to and buy property.

This book includes an area design for more interesting inclusive life, and to help people be part of it's design forever, helping create a better more meaningful feeling of life. To open up work options for people and make work feel more rewarding.

A note before reading

This is a book of ideas — some carefully developed, some written down in the moment and left as they came. It is part proposal and part personal journal, and I have not fact-checked or researched the claims it makes.

You will find ideas for community design, inventors' organisations, casual work, and city planning alongside more personal writing about isolation, work, and frustration. Some passages are harsh or one-sided. I don't actually believe people, government, or daily life are as bad as I sometimes write them — that is how things felt on particular days, not how I think they are in general. If negative views of work, society, or other people are not what you came for, the more personal sections are easier to skip than to argue with.

If anything here is useful, take it. The rest you can leave.

=======

Limit prices to construction costs

“Specific non-profit, cooperative, and government-subsidized models exist where home prices are limited to, or closely tied to, the actual cost of construction and development.

Here are the contexts in which this occurs:

1. Community Land Trusts (CLTs)

In a Community Land Trust, the organization owns the land, and the individual owns only the structure.

  • Mechanism: When the home is sold, a formula limits the resale price to the original construction cost plus restricted appreciation (or sometimes just the original cost).
  • Location: Primarily in the United States, United Kingdom, and parts of Canada, though this model is growing globally. This specifically removes the "land value" speculation from the sales price.

2. Housing Cooperatives (e.g., Zurich, Switzerland)

Switzerland, particularly Zurich, has a large non-profit housing sector (cooperatives) that operates on a "cost-rent" or cost-price basis.

  • Mechanism: Members pay for the construction, maintenance, and financing costs, not market rate rent or resale value.
  • Structure: Because they are non-profit, the homes are not subject to the speculative pressures of the broader land market.

3. Government-Subsidized "Cost-Price" Models

Some governments directly manage housing development where the sale price is strictly controlled to be based on the construction cost.

  • Singapore (HDB): While not exclusively just construction cost, the Housing & Development Board (HDB) prices new flats based on the cost of building, rather than market value, offering subsidies to keep them affordable.
  • Former Social Economies: In some socialist economies, housing was allocated based on construction costs, although this is rare in modern free-market contexts.”

“1. The academic version (very close to that idea)

People “vote with their feet”

They move to communities that match their preferences (taxes, lifestyle, services)

Over time → people sort into like-minded groups

👉 That is basically the same core idea as the website you sent.

studying how people sort into neighborhoods

even applying it to online communities

2. Real-world versions already exist

Intentional communities / communes

People deliberately live together based on shared values

This has existed for hundreds of year

Examples include:

eco villages

religious communities

cooperative housing

Cohousing (modern version)

Private homes + shared spaces

Self-governed communities

Forming your own local council

Local Government is the sphere of government which most directly affects people. States are divided into local areas, each of which is governed by an individual authority, known as a Council. Council activities include waste management, local environmental management, local roads, town planning, parks, libraries, social planning and many other services. Otherwise called District, Town or City Councils.

Important

You will need to do this in order implement city experiments  

How to

Either by

  • getting elected by local council
  • making a new council within an area by taking a petition containing the signatures of at least 7.5% of the local population.
  • Making a new area by moving with people who believe in something and making a new partition to form a new council, the number of people who sign the partition may be between 100 to 2500 depending on country

What you get

Then you can more easily design a city

The bystander effect


“The bystander effect is a social psychological phenomenon where individuals are less likely to offer help to a victim when other people are present, as the likelihood of intervention decreases as the group size increases. Primarily driven by a diffusion of responsibility and fear of judgment, this inaction stems from assuming others will act or that the situation is not an emergency.”

“The bystander effect has been proven hundreds of times. Your brain is made to hold small tribes of a couple hundred people and the moment that tribe expands into something your brain can't imagine you are no longer relying on reputation from anyone. You don't care what other people are thinking about you. And the moment that stops your brain says, "I don't have the capacity to worry about everyone that I see." So empathy disappears. Like you walk down these streets here in New York, their empathy is zero for you. No matter what's happening, you walk through a country town that's like 1,500 people. The population of the town I live in is 2,200. And if you get cut on the armor like you stumbled, four cars will stop. People get out of their cars to figure out what's going on because our brains can handle smaller tribes. The moment we get flooded with all of these things, all of these people that we can't possibly care about everybody, empathy disappears. The second aspect of this is if we're surrounded by environments that our ancestors would be absolutely scared of and confused by. We we start developing problems in our brain. Depression, loneliness, suicide through the roof in large cities every time. There's no exception. “

#Necessities1121 1

“You ever heard it said that we live in the most advanced society in human history, but somehow half of us can't afford rent, can't see a doctor, and think meal prep means choosing which bill not to pay so we can buy groceries.

Welcome to “Maslow's hierarchy of needs”, brought to you by Late-stage Capitalism. where the only thing self-actualizing is corporate profits and everyone else is just trying not to scream in public.

At level one of Maslow's pyramid, the base, the part with things like food and shelter and not dying.
If you're unfamiliar with Maslau's hierarchy of needs, it's a psychological theory that explains human motivations as a five level pyramid. And at the base are physiological needs.
1. Things like food, water, sleep, and shelter. You know, the absolute essentials. If those aren't met, nothing else really matters.
2. Next is safety. having a stable home, access to health care, financial security and protection from harm.
3. Then next comes love and belonging, relationships, friendships, community. Above that is esteem, feeling respected, competent and valued.
4. And then at the top is self-actualization. The drive to fulfill your potential, create and live with purpose.

So the idea is pretty simple. You can't focus on becoming your best self if you're too busy trying to survive. And right now, a lot of people can't even get past level one. Many of us are nonetheless trying to accomplish things higher up the pyramid without having established the essential needs at the bottom. And this is resulting in a great deal of suffering in our modern lives. “

The New Atlantis

“THE NEW ATLANTIS by Sir Francis Bacon - 1627”http://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2434
This is a book about a town in USA in 1627 that collected invention, technology, material for the development of their invention and development  

For the several employments and offices of our fellows; we have twelve that sail into foreign countries, under the names of other nations, (for our own we conceal); who bring us the books, and abstracts, and patterns of experiments of all other parts. These we call Merchants of Light.

We have three that collect the experiments which are in all books. These we call Experiment Researchers.

We have three that collect the experiments of all mechanical arts; and also of liberal sciences; and also of practices which are not brought into arts. These we call Mystery Researchers.

We have three that try new experiments, such as themselves think good. These we call Pioneers.

We have three that draw the experiments of the former four into titles and tables, to give the better light for the drawing of observations and axioms out of them. These we call Compilers.

We have three that bend themselves, looking into the experiments of their fellows, and cast about how to draw out of them things of use and practise for man's life, and knowledge, as well for works as for plain demonstration of causes, means of natural divinations, and the easy and clear discovery of the virtues and parts of bodies. These we call Benefactors.

Then after divers meetings and consults of our whole number, to consider of the former labours and collections, we have three that take care, out of them, to direct new experiments, of a higher light, more penetrating into nature than the former. These we call Lamps.

We have three others that do execute the experiments so directed, and report them. These we call Inoculators.

Lastly, we have three that raise the former discoveries by experiments into greater observations, axioms, and aphorisms. These we call Interpreters of Nature.

We have consultations, which of the inventions and experiences which we have discovered shall be published, and which not: and take all an oath of secrecy, for the concealing of those which we think fit to keep secret: though some of those we do reveal sometimes to the state and some not.

For our ordinances and rites: we have two very long and fair galleries: in one of these we place patterns and samples of all manner of the more rare and excellent inventions in the other we place the statues of all principal inventors. There we have the statue of your Columbus, that discovered the West Indies: also the inventor of ships: your monk that was the inventor of ordnance and of gunpowder: the inventor of music: the inventor of letters: the inventor of printing: the inventor of observations of astronomy: the inventor of works in metal: the inventor of glass: the inventor of silk of the worm: the inventor of wine: the inventor of corn and bread: the inventor of sugars: and all these, by more certain tradition than you have. Then have we divers inventors of our own, of excellent works; which since you have not seen, it were too long to make descriptions of them; and besides, in the right understanding of those descriptions you might easily err. For upon every invention of value, we erect a statue to the inventor, and give him a liberal and honourable reward.

We do publish such new profitable inventions as we think good. And we do also declare natural divinations of diseases, plagues, swarms-of hurtful creatures, scarcity, tempests, earthquakes, great inundations, comets, temperature of the year, and divers other things; and we give counsel thereupon, what the people shall do for the prevention and remedy of them.

We have certain hymns and services, which we say daily, of Lord and thanks to God for his marvellous works: and forms of prayers, imploring his aid and blessing for the illumination of our labours, and the turning of them into good and holy uses.

We have also a mathematical house, where are represented all instruments, as well of geometry as astronomy, exquisitely made

We have also houses of deceits of the senses; where we represent all manner of feats of juggling, false apparitions, impostures, and illusions; and their fallacies. And surely you will easily believe that we that have so many things truly natural which induce admiration, could in a world of particulars deceive the senses, if we would disguise those things and labour to make them seem more miraculous. But we do hate all impostures, and lies; insomuch as we have severely forbidden it to all our fellows, under pain of ignominy and fines, that they do not show any natural work or thing, adorned or swelling; but only pure as it is, and without all affectation of strangeness.

We have also engine-houses, where are prepared engines and instruments for all sorts of motions. There we imitate and practise to make swifter motions than any you have, either out of your muskets or any engine that you have: and to make them and multiply them more easily, and with small force, by wheels and other means: and to make them stronger and more violent than yours are; exceeding your greatest cannons and basilisks. We represent also ordnance and instruments of war, and engines of all kinds: and likewise new mixtures and compositions of gun-powder, wild-fires burning in water, and unquenchable. Also fireworks of all variety both for pleasure and use. We imitate also flights of birds; we have some degrees of flying in the air. We have ships and boats for going under water, and brooking of seas; also swimming-girdles and supporters. We have divers curious clocks, and other like motions of return: and some perpetual motions. We imitate also motions of living creatures, by images, of men, beasts, birds, fishes, and serpents. We have also a great number of other various motions, strange for equality, fineness, and subtilty.

We have also sound-houses, where we practise and demonstrate all sounds, and their generation. We have harmonies which you have not, of quarter-sounds, and lesser slides of sounds. Divers instruments of music likewise to you unknown, some sweeter than any you have, together with bells and rings that are dainty and sweet. We represent small sounds as great and deep; likewise great sounds extenuate and sharp; we make divers tremblings and warblings of sounds, which in their original are entire. We represent and imitate all articulate sounds and letters, and the voices and notes of beasts and birds. We have certain helps which set to the ear do further the hearing greatly. We have also divers strange and artificial echoes, reflecting the voice many times, and as it were tossing it: and some that give back the voice louder than it came, some shriller, and some deeper; yea, some rendering the voice differing in the letters or articulate sound from that they receive. We have also means to convey sounds in trunks and pipes, in strange lines and distances.

We have dispensatories, or shops of medicines. Wherein you may easily think, if we have such variety of plants and living creatures more than you have in Europe, (for we know what you have,) the simples, drugs, and ingredients of medicines, must likewise be in so much the greater variety. We have them likewise of divers ages, and long fermentations. And for their preparations, we have not only all manner of exquisite distillations and separations, and especially by gentle heats and percolations through divers strainers, yea and substances; but also exact forms of composition, whereby they incorporate almost, as they were natural simples.

We have also divers mechanical arts, which you have not; and stuffs made by them; as papers, linen, silks, tissues; dainty works of feathers of wonderful lustre; excellent dies, and, many others; and shops likewise, as well for such as are not brought into vulgar use amongst us as for those that are. For you must know that of the things before recited, many of them are grown into use throughout the kingdom; but yet, if they did flow from our invention, we have of them also for patterns and principals.

We have also furnaces of great diversities, and that keep great diversity of heats; fierce and quick; strong and constant; soft and mild; blown, quiet; dry, moist; and the like. But above all, we have heats, in imitation of the Sun's and heavenly bodies' heats, that pass divers inequalities, and (as it were) orbs, progresses, and returns, whereby we produce admirable effects. Besides, we have heats of dungs; and of bellies and maws of living creatures, and of their bloods and bodies; and of hays and herbs laid up moist; of lime unquenched; and such like. Instruments also which generate heat only by motion. And farther, places for strong insulations; and again, places under the earth, which by nature, or art, yield heat. These divers heats we use, as the nature of the operation, which we intend, requireth.

We have also perspective-houses, where we make demonstrations of all lights and radiations; and of all colours: and out of things uncoloured and transparent, we can represent unto you all several colours; not in rain-bows, (as it is in gems, and prisms,) but of themselves single. We represent also all multiplications of light, which we carry to great distance, and make so sharp as to discern small points and lines. Also all colourations of light; all delusions and deceits of the sight, in figures, magnitudes, motions, colours all demonstrations of shadows. We find also divers means, yet unknown to you, of producing of light originally from divers bodies. We procure means of seeing objects afar off; as in the heaven and remote places; and represent things near as afar off; and things afar off as near; making feigned distances. We have also helps for the sight, far above spectacles and glasses in use. We have also glasses and means to see small and minute bodies perfectly and distinctly; as the shapes and colours of small flies and worms, grains and flaws in gems, which cannot otherwise be seen, observations in urine and blood not otherwise to be seen. We make artificial rain-bows, halo's, and circles about light. We represent also all manner of reflexions, refractions, and multiplications of visual beams of objects.

The bystander effect


“The bystander effect is a social psychological phenomenon where individuals are less likely to offer help to a victim when other people are present, as the likelihood of intervention decreases as the group size increases. Primarily driven by a diffusion of responsibility and fear of judgment, this inaction stems from assuming others will act or that the situation is not an emergency.”

“The bystander effect has been proven hundreds of times. Your brain is made to hold small tribes of a couple hundred people and the moment that tribe expands into something your brain can't imagine you are no longer relying on reputation from anyone. You don't care what other people are thinking about you. And the moment that stops your brain says, "I don't have the capacity to worry about everyone that I see." So empathy disappears. Like you walk down these streets here in New York, their empathy is zero for you. No matter what's happening, you walk through a country town that's like 1,500 people. The population of the town I live in is 2,200. And if you get cut on the armor like you stumbled, four cars will stop. People get out of their cars to figure out what's going on because our brains can handle smaller tribes. The moment we get flooded with all of these things, all of these people that we can't possibly care about everybody, empathy disappears. The second aspect of this is if we're surrounded by environments that our ancestors would be absolutely scared of and confused by. We we start developing problems in our brain. Depression, loneliness, suicide through the roof in large cities every time. There's no exception. “

Looking at data from Adelaide or Australia can you find something that's going to go wrong that hasn't been described yet, e.g. they are building in an area that will be flooded in 20 years but no one figured that out yet

“Riverlea, north of Adelaide — a 35,000-person town being built now on the flat Gawler River floodplain, ~2.7 km from the coast.

The river flood risk is old news: it was modelled back when the site was called Buckland Park, the 2016 flood review ran "with development" scenarios, and locals raised concerns publicly years ago. None of that is new.

The only possibly-undescribed angle is narrower — and unconfirmed: the floodplain drains to the sea by gravity, but that coast is both rising (sea level) and sinking (subsidence). If the flood model assumed today's sea level at the outfall, floodwater could sit deeper and longer in later decades than the maps show. But that interaction might already be inside the model — I found a plausible gap, not a proven one.

Honest bottom line: finding a risk no expert has spotted is very hard from public data. The realistic version is spotting known risks that may not have been combined properly, then checking. The FOI request above asks the one question that settles it: static or rising sea boundary? If it's already accounted for, there's no story.”

Anything completely unique and missed by humans

I think if I asked you to examine more data, standard data that it will be too much data and too much time looking for something

I can't find something no human has ever seen — I read the same public data everyone else does, no secret feeds. Anything I surface has already been seen by someone.

My only real edge is cheap cross-domain joining: stitching together fields whose experts don't read each other's work (flood engineer + subsidence geologist + planner + tide-gauge scientist). That seam is where the Riverlea idea came from — and also why I couldn't prove it was actually missed.

You're also right that brute-force scanning won't help — more data buries the signal. What works is a sharp hypothesis pointing at exactly which two layers to overlay, then one check.

Bottom line: I can hand you a testable mismatch and the single query that settles it — not a certified novel discovery. Point me at a domain you care about and I'll aim one sharp guess at it.

A game about augmented support life

Continued from above here are some more ideas. Ideas were continuation of idea list made by someone who took all the ideas from Microsoft Hololens ideas completion website and listed the titles (the descriptions are my own, as Microsoft has removed the list 6 months later and I have not spent time looking for the archive on archive.org).

Find other ideas on the internet about ways to use hololens and add as ideas for the game.

In no particular order.

1.       Allow you to view your videogame character in 3D space and inspect them, or their inventories

2.       Holographic UI to assist in playing a game

3.       Instant board / table-top games with other people using HoloLens

4.       Play virtual sports (real or fake, like Quidditch)

5.       Geo-based holograph reality game (requires 4G/LTE HoloLens)

6.       Insane horror game

7.       Virtual legos/Minecraft in 3D space

8.       Helping kids with autism with a “social avatar buddy”

9.       To-do list (to-do’s all over)

10.   Cooking companion (visualize recipes)

11.   Virtual decorations for your house (“Decoration Store”)

12.   HoloLens restaurant

13.   Visualize how to decorate your home (“Oh the couch would look nice here”)

14.   Photos on the wall

15.   Running apps — rendered zombies or whatever behind you

16.   Inspecting your car (what is this? where is this?)

17.   Car windshields equipped with holo display

18.   HoloContacts — eventually HoloLens inside a contact lens

19.   Virtual partner

20.   Visualizing clothing or haircut

21.   Google Earth/StreetView for low-cost travel

22.   Wall-sized environments ala Hunger Games wall (forest, lakes, beach, etc.)

23.   Reading a book to your kid (project pages in space/onto wall)

24.   Virtual reading / bookshelf (reach out, take a virtual book, hold and read/flip pages)

25.   Holo Sims game (lonely? get a roommate)

26.   Cortana in person

27.   Virtual window weather app—so the window reflects what it’s like outside

28.   Pin specific types of news stories

29.   Fridge pinning

30.   Virtual pinned calendar for easy planning

31.   Pin your kids’ projects on the fridge (teacher saves through Internet => home)

32.   Rotating posters or /r/aww or awwpets.com on your wall

33.   On your fridge, post what you eat/or say it and view it right there

34.   Object recognition for food in fridge/pantry —> pantry app, “Cortana, what do I need to make Beef Stroganoff?”

35.   Pin shows in Netflix near TV so I can tap and watch/resume

36.   Portable screen for playing games (LAN parties anyone?)

37.   Ceiling craziness (skyboxes, night sky)

38.   Live holo concerts

39.   Holo Videos — videos shot in 3D space (HoloTV, HoloTube, etc.)

Painkillers

“Almost everything we think we know about addiction is wrong. You get a rat and you put it in a cage and you give it two water bottles. One is just water and the other is water laced with either heroin or cocaine. If you do that, the rat will almost always prefer the drug water and almost always kill itself quite quickly.

In the 70s, Professor Alexander comes along and he looks at this experiment and he noticed something. He said, "Ah, we're putting the rat in an empty cage.

It's got nothing to do except use these drugs. Let's try something a bit different." So, Professor Alexander built a cage that he called Rat Park.

They've got loads of cheese. They've got loads of colored balls. They've got loads of tunnels. Crucially, they've got loads of friends. But here's the fascinating thing. In Rat Park, they don't like the drug water. You go from almost 100% overdose when they're isolated to 0% overdose when they have happy and connected lives. What if addiction isn't about your chemical hooks? What if addiction is about your cage? What if addiction is an adaptation to your environment? Maybe we shouldn't even call it addiction. Maybe we should call it bonding. Human beings have a natural and innate need to bond. And when we're happy and healthy, we'll bond and connect with each other. But if you can't do that because you're traumatized or isolated or beaten down by life, you will bond with something that will give you some sense of relief. Now, that might be gambling, that might be pornography, that might be cocaine, that might be cannabis, but you will bond and connect with something because that's our nature. The opposite of addiction is not sobriety. The opposite of addiction is connection.”

For did not Christ set a little child in the midst of the disciples, saying to them that the angels of such little ones always behold the face of His father; saying to them that it were better for a man to hang a millstone about his neck and plunge into the uttermost depths of the sea than to injure such a little one?

And what to-day is the result of private property in land in the richest of so called Christian countries? Is it not that young people fear to marry; that married people fear to have children; that children are driven out of life from sheer want of proper nourishment and care, or compelled to toil when they ought to be at school or at play; that great numbers of those who attain maturity enter it with under-nourished bodies, overstrained nerves, undeveloped minds—under conditions that foredoom them, not merely to suffering, but to crime; that fit them in advance for the prison and the brothel?

If your Holiness will consider these things we are confident that instead of defending private property in land you will condemn it with anathema!”

“ George Carlin warned us. It's called the American dream because you have to be asleep to believe it. And we were. But now everyone's half awake staring around at the smoldering ruins and thinking, "So what now?"

“ Now we used to have reality and then we outsourced it to screens. Now everything is theater, politics, morality, uh even grief. We um basically turned existence into a brand campaign. The Republic didn't fall.

It just got a new logo and a Tik Tok strategy. So Gabbor called this the society of the spectacle and he wrote about this back in the 1960s. And this is where image replaces truth and the performance becomes more real than the thing it's imitating.

So we used to experience the world but now we just experience our reaction to it. We don't really live, we comment on living. Um elections feel like product launches. Tragedies get edited into um short form empathy clips. Um protests have sponsorship deals.

“Long-term Stockholm syndrome causes severe, enduring mental and physical health effects, often mirroring PTSD, including chronic anxiety, depression, deep-seated trust issues, and potential cardiovascular problems. Survivors may suffer from low self-esteem, flashbacks, and cognitive distortions that complicate recovery, while physical symptoms like chronic fatigue, headaches, or gastrointestinal issues can persist long after the abusive situation ends.

Mental and Psychological Health Effects

  • PTSD and Anxiety: Survivors often experience intense fear, flashbacks, nightmares, and chronic anxiety, similar to PTSD symptoms, as reported on the Cleveland Clinic website.
  • Depression and Dissociation: Long-term depression and dissociation (numbness) are common as survivors process the traumatic experience, notes the Medical News Today article.
  • Cognitive Distortions: Survivors may continue to hold positive feelings toward their captor, minimize the abuse, or feel responsible for their own victimization, explains this article on Healthline.
  • Trust and Attachment Issues: Establishing healthy relationships becomes challenging due to deep-seated distrust and, in some cases, a tendency to repeat abusive relationship patterns, according to the ChoosingTherapy.com article and a 2025 study mentioned by Still Mind Florida.

Physical Health Consequences

  • Chronic Stress Disorders: The sustained, high-level stress of captivity can lead to long-term health issues such as chronic headaches, digestive problems, and cardiovascular dysfunction, reports ChoosingTherapy.com.
  • Cardiovascular Risks: Research on traumatic stress indicates that survivors with PTSD have an increased risk of hypertension and chronic heart disease, notes the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
  • Physical Exhaustion: Persistent fatigue and insomnia are frequently reported long-term symptoms, says the NCBI report.

Recovery Challenges

  • Difficulty Seeking Help: Due to the bond formed with the captor, survivors might be hesitant to seek help or legal action, or may, according to a case study from the NIH, experience increased empathy toward the abuser after the threat passes.
  • Long-term Therapy Needed: Treatment often requires long-term psychotherapy to address the complex trauma, rebuild self-esteem, and establish healthy coping mechanisms, say experts at Healthline.

In addition to these effects, survivors may also experience a "foreshortened future," where they have limited, pessimistic expectations about their life and future opportunities, according to the NCBI report. “

“Humans are social animals. The need to belong is deeply ingrained-we need to feel a sense of connection and belonging. Being part of something bigger can help give meaning to our lives, linding and spending time with other people with the same values, Interests and views makes us feel valued and we realise that we're not alone

Feeling disconnected from others can deeply affect our self-perception and emotional health. Some studies have linked the emotional effects of social isolation to physical illness including heart disease, weakened immunity and even premature death.

The benefits of a sense of community go further than avoiding loneliness. Belonging to a group we can identify with helps us develop a stronger sense of our own identity. It boosts self-esteem and gives us the courage to take on the world and make our dreams. happen

And it helps our emotional development, Sharing is caring the positive emotions and empowerment we feel when we share are a huge benefit to mental health. The more we interact with people in our comumumiy

the more we learn, the more we practice acceptance which in turn helps us with self-acceptance

There are opportunities all around us to build meaningful human relationships and benefit from the healing power that comes with a sense of community. It's just a matter of opening our eyes to them.”

“ Why calm takes time? Why the nervous

 system doesn't trust peace immediately.

 Calm is often described as the absence

 of threat. But biologically calm is

 something that must be learned. A

 nervous system shaped by survival

 doesn't relax just because danger is

 gone. It relaxes when safety becomes

 predictable. For a tired nervous system,

 calm is unfamiliar territory. Alertness

 kept you alive. Tension created control.

 Stillness meant vulnerability.

 So when the body begins to slow down,

 the system asks, "Is this safe or is

 this when something happens?" This is

 why rest can feel uneasy, why silence

 creates anxiety, why calm doesn't feel

 calming at first. Calm is a biological

 update. The nervous system doesn't

 change through insight. It changes

 through repetition.

 Repeated moments where nothing bad

 happens while the body is at ease. This

 is not mindset work. This is exposure.

 Small doses of safety repeated without

 forcing.

 Why it takes time? Because the system is

 not broken. It is cautious. It learned

 that vigilance mattered and it doesn't

 forget that overnight calm becomes

 available only after the body learns.

 Nothing is required of me right now.

 Nothing is about to collapse. Not

 pushing relaxation. Not performing

 stillness, but consistency,

 regular rhythms, gentle transitions,

 predictable rest. Calm doesn't arrive

 dramatically. It arrives quietly when

 the nervous system stops checking the

 exits.

 If calm feels distant, you are not

 failing. Your body is learning what

 safety feels like. Now, next episode,

 what safety does to cognition?

 Why thinking changes after the body

 settles. “

 Brain Lion Institute episode 49.

“ What safety does to cognition? How

 thinking changes after the body settles.

 We often think thinking happens in the

 brain. But biologically thinking depends

 on safety, not comfort, not positivity,

 safety.

 Cognition is not a purely mental

 process. Your brain doesn't think in

 isolation. It thinks inside a body that

 is constantly asking one question. Is it

 safe enough to process more? When the

 answer is no, cognition changes. Not

 because you are incapable, but because

 resources are limited. What happens when

 safety is low? In survival states,

 attention narrows. Thinking becomes

 repetitive.

 Creativity drops. Memory prioritizes

 stress. The future feels abstract or

 unreachable. This is not a mindset

 problem. This is a resource allocation

 strategy. The brain shifts from

 exploration to prediction, from learning

 to protection. When the nervous system

 begins to feel safe, blood flow

 redistributes.

 Oxygen availability increases. Glucose

 use becomes more efficient.

 The preffrontal cortex comes back

 online. This is when reflection becomes

 possible. Nuance returns. Long-term

 thinking reappears.

 Insight feels effortless. Not because

 you tried harder, but because the system

 allowed it. You cannot think your way

 into biological safety. The brain

 doesn't respond to instructions. It

 responds to conditions.

 When safety is inconsistent, clarity

 feels fragile. When safety stabilizes,

 clarity becomes natural.

 The key shift, cognition improves after

 regulation, not before it. This is why

 rest, rhythm, and nervous system support

 often unlock understanding without

 effort.

 If your thinking feels foggy, flat, or

 stuck, it doesn't mean you are failing.

 It may mean your system hasn't felt safe

 long enough to think freely yet.

 Next episode, the blood brain barrier

 where protection shapes perception. “

AI Overview:

Yes, research strongly indicates that people are generally more productive, engaged, and satisfied with their lives when they work around friends

 or have close, positive relationships with colleagues. Having a "best friend" at work is linked to higher employee engagement, increased innovation, and a significantly lower likelihood of leaving a job. Forbes +5

Impact on Well-being and Job Satisfaction

  • Reduced Stress & Burnout: Workplace friendships act as a support system, reducing cortisol levels and helping employees manage stress from demanding jobs or difficult managers.
  • Increased Happiness: Having friends makes the workday more enjoyable, with 57% of workers saying it improves their overall job satisfaction.
  • Reduced Loneliness: With many people spending a third of their lives at work, friendships combat isolation, which is linked to better mental health and lower absenteeism.
  • Higher Retention: Employees with friends at work are 30% less likely to quit, as they feel more emotionally attached to their team and organization. Forbes +4

Impact on Productivity and Performance

  • Higher Engagement: Employees with a "best friend" at work are seven times more likely to be engaged in their work, often leading to better customer service and higher quality work.
  • Better Collaboration: Friends in the workplace communicate more openly, share feedback more freely, and are more likely to support each other on projects.
  • Efficiency Gains: Although socializing can sometimes take time, the increased motivation, reduced turnover, and improved collaboration often lead to higher overall productivity. Forbes +5

Potential Risks and Considerations

While generally positive, workplace friendships can have downsides if not managed well:

  • Distractions: Socializing can sometimes cause distractions and reduce focus on immediate tasks.
  • Favoritism & Cliques: Close friendships may create perceptions of favoritism or lead to the exclusion of other team members.
  • Conflict Spillover: Personal conflicts between friends can sometimes affect the work environment. Leigh Morrison +3

Key Takeaways for Success

To maximize the benefits of workplace friendships, experts suggest:

  • Setting Boundaries: Maintaining professionalism while being friendly is key to avoiding conflicts of interest, especially with supervisors.
  • Encouraging Inclusivity: Ensuring friendships do not create exclusive "cliques" in the office.
  • Fostering a Social Environment: Leaders can support these relationships through team-building activities, social events, and encouraging collaboration.

The Australian Government provides a range of financial incentives and support mechanisms aimed at encouraging businesses to hire, boosting skills through apprenticeships, and improving workplace well-being. As of 2026, these initiatives are heavily focused on critical sectors like housing and clean energy, while also supporting vulnerable job seekers and ensuring mental health and flexibility in the workplace.

Here are the key government incentives and initiatives:

1. Hiring and Employment Incentives (Wage Subsidies)

The government provides financial assistance to employers to reduce the cost of hiring and training, especially for long-term unemployed or disadvantaged individuals.

  • Wage Subsidies (up to $10,000): Provided to businesses that hire eligible individuals (including youth under 24, Indigenous Australians, parents, and those registered with employment providers for over 6 months) for ongoing positions.
  • Restart Wage Subsidy ($10,000): Aimed at employers hiring eligible job seekers aged 50 and over.
  • Inclusive Employment Australia: Offers wage subsidies and support for hiring people with disabilities.
  • Transition to Work: Supports young people (15-24) by helping them prepare for work, including wage subsidies of up to $10,000 for employers. Job Access +6

2. Apprenticeship and Training Support (2026 Focus)

From January 1, 2026, the government has updated its apprenticeship incentives, targeting critical industries like housing and clean energy to create sustainable jobs. Apprenticeship Support Australia +1

  • Key Apprenticeship Program (KAP): Employers can receive up to $5,000 for taking on apprentices in priority housing and clean energy roles (e.g., electricians, plumbers).
  • Apprentice Support (KAP): Apprentices in these priority areas can receive up to $10,000.
  • Priority Hiring Incentive: For non-KAP priority occupations, employers may receive up to $2,500.
  • Australian Apprenticeship Support Loans: Interest-free loans of up to $25,983 (2025-26) to help apprentices with living costs, with a 20% discount on completion.
  • Living Away From Home Allowance (LAFHA): Tax-free payments for apprentices forced to move for their training.
  • Disability Australian Apprentice Wage Support (DAAWS): Up to $216.07 per week for employers supporting apprentices with disabilities.
  • Free TAFE: Continues to reduce training costs for priority skills areas. Apprenticeship Support Australia +4

3. Workplace Well-being and Culture Improvements

To make people happier at work and promote mental health, the government supports various initiatives:

  • Psychosocial Hazard Regulation (NSW 2026): Stricter enforcement of work health and safety laws to address workplace bullying, harassment, and burnout.
  • Employee Assistance Program (EAP): Support for employers to provide confidential counseling for employees and their families.
  • Mental Health Support for Emergency Workers: Specific grants (e.g., over $19 million to Fortem Australia) for mental health services.
  • Flexible Work Arrangements: Promotion of hybrid work and flexible hours to improve work-life balance.
  • Gender Equity and Safety: Initiatives such as the Building Women’s Careers Program to address gender imbalances and improve workplace safety. nema.gov.au +5

4. Supporting Remote and Specialized Employment

  • Remote Australia Employment Service: Tailored support for finding work in regional and remote areas.
  • Self-Employment Assistance: Provides training and mentoring for those looking to start their own business. Department of Employment and Workplace Relations +4

5. Paid Parental Leave (2026 Changes)

To improve work-life balance for families, the government is expanding the Paid Parental Leave scheme.

  • 26 Weeks Leave (from July 1, 2026): The scheme increases to 26 weeks, with 4 weeks reserved for each parent to encourage shared care ("use it or lose it" component).
  • Superannuation on PPL: Government-funded superannuation contributions on paid parental leave continue. Keypoint Law

These measures aim to create a more resilient, skilled, and satisfied workforce while easing the financial burden on employers.

UV radiation damages folate and nails primarily through photolysis and oxidative stress, causing molecular-level degradation and structural weakening.

No, a standard blood test in Australia does not specifically test for "folate damage" caused by sun UV radiation.

Yes, you can experience folate (vitamin B9) damage or degradation from sun exposure without being sunburnt.

 “UV radiation isn't just uncomfortable. It's destructive at the molecular level. It breaks chemical bonds. It damages DNA. Most critically for our ancestors, it destroys folate, a B vitamin absolutely essential for human survival. Folate does something remarkable. It protects DNA during cell division, especially during the rapid cell division that happens when embryos are forming. Without adequate folate, neural tubes don't close properly. Spines don't form correctly. Pregnancies fail. Even in adults, folate deficiency causes anemia, weakness, the inability to heal wounds properly. In the harsh environment of prehistoric Africa, folate deficiency was a death sentence. The African sun destroys folate. Studies show that just a few hours of intense UV exposure can degrade folate levels in the bloodstream by more than half. Now imagine you're an early human spending 12 hours a day outside hunting, gathering, traveling between water sources. Without protection, your folate reserves would be depleted constantly. Enter melanin, nature's perfect sunscreen. “

Regarding ghost town investment

So there are some large areas like ghost towns but somehow not for sale

Refusal to Privatise: In some areas, local governments historically did not allow residents to privatise their homes, leading to a situation where the state owns the land while individuals may still hold rights to crumbling buildings.

Dismantled Assets: During the economic shifts of the 1990s, residents often dismantled buildings to sell the wood and metal for survival, leaving behind "zombie" titles that are legally messy to consolidate for a single investor.

Complex Restitutions: After 1991, property was returned to the descendants of owners from the 1920s. These owners may live abroad and have no interest in selling, but also no funds to restore.

Heritage Protection: Many are listed as national monuments, meaning an investor cannot just "buy" and develop them without massive, state-regulated restoration costs that often exceed the property's value.

Housing and food are basic needs

The phrase "Give us this day our daily bread" originated in Judea (modern-day Israel and the Palestinian Territories) approximately 2,000 years ago.

And people are still saying it today.

Over the course of a lifetime in 100 BC Judea, food was significantly more expensive than housing, typically consuming 50% or more of a person's total lifetime earnings.

In the present day, housing has definitively overtaken food as the most expensive lifetime cost—a complete reversal from 2,000 years ago.

But they didn't change the prayer.

State control

Most Australians live in one dominant city per state because the system rewards concentration. Each state runs its hospitals, universities, courts, and transport out of the capital, so jobs and services cluster there, and restrictive state planning makes it hard for regional centres to grow into real alternatives. Federal money follows the votes, which are already in the capital, reinforcing the pattern.

  • NSW → Sydney (~two-thirds of the state)
  • Victoria → Melbourne (~three-quarters)
  • Queensland → Brisbane (~half, though the coast also has Gold Coast and Sunshine Coast)
  • Western Australia → Perth (over 80%)
  • South Australia → Adelaide (~77%)
  • Tasmania → Hobart
  • Northern Territory → Darwin
  • ACT → Canberra

This pattern isn't an accident — it's actively reinforced by how states plan and spend.

 Regarding “vote with your feet” by AI chatbot

The idea — many small jurisdictions, people sort themselves into the one that fits — was formalised by economist Charles Tiebout in 1956. If governments have to compete for residents, they have to earn their stay through good services, sensible taxes, and rules people actually want.

**Where it works well:**

- **Experimentation.** Small places can try different tax, planning, or welfare systems. The rest copy what works and learn from what fails.

- **Accountability.** Governments that can lose residents have to perform.

- **Matching.** Low-tax-low-service types and high-tax-high-service types can each live somewhere that fits.

- **Genuine variety.** Different communities can sustain different ways of life rather than everyone being squeezed into one national average.

Switzerland (26 cantons, 9 million people) is the textbook success — wealthy, stable, with real cantonal autonomy on tax, schools, and healthcare delivery. Germany and parts of the US show similar patterns at a larger scale.

**Where it goes wrong:**

- **Sorting by wealth.** People don't just sort by preference, they sort by income. Rich jurisdictions get richer, poor ones get hollowed out. American school funding is the classic example.

- **Race to the bottom.** Competition can drive down standards on environmental rules, worker protections, and corporate tax. Each state undercuts the others; everyone ends up worse.

- **Coordination failures.** Pollution, disease, water, climate, infrastructure all cross borders. Small jurisdictions can't solve them alone.

- **Mobility is unequal.** "Voting with your feet" assumes you can move. Poor, sick, elderly, and rooted people can't.

- **Capture.** Small places are easier for local elites to dominate than large ones. "Local control" sometimes means local oligarchy.

**What makes the difference:** The successful decentralised countries all have the same guardrails — strong national protection of individual rights, fiscal transfers from rich to poor jurisdictions, free internal movement, and national rules preventing the worst competitive behaviour. Decentralisation without those guardrails produces the bad version: fragmented, unequal, captured.

**For Australia:** The country is genuinely too centralised for its size. States have responsibility without revenue and the Commonwealth meddles in things it doesn't understand. But creating new states is politically near-impossible. A more realistic version of the same intuition: let local councils and regional authorities set their own planning rules, their own surcharges, their own service mixes — experimentation within states, rather than splitting them.

**So would more, smaller states be better?**

Done well, with the guardrails — yes, probably. More experimentation, more matching, more accountability, less of the trapped-in-one-system feeling the book complains about.

Done badly, without guardrails — you'd swap one problem for another: sorting by wealth, weakened protections, local capture.

"Decentralisation" isn't a single policy. It's a design problem. The same word covers Switzerland and the worst parts of pre-civil-rights America. What matters is what you keep central and what you devolve — and almost nobody in the public conversation distinguishes those carefully.

I dislike schedules so much that I go online to find a doctor available in the next few hours on the booking system HotDoc, and I'll go anywhere not too far away.

I thought, if I were a doctor or something, I would only allow booking this way — for the few hours that day that I wanted to work.

Idea: "in-line" booking — scheduling without a set time for the "things to do" app. When you set your profile to active, booking is an expression of interest in seeing that person. When they go online and you're also online and you're next in the queue, you get a notification that a time is available in 1–2 hours. The next people in the queue are given this option a minute after the first, but the option stays open in your "things to do" app until someone takes the appointment.

It's good for someone who wants to work when they want, but also wants people lined up for work. It's an important concept for the gig or casual work section I was writing about before: having a queue indicates whether there's work or not, rather than just going online to see.
